title: LinkedIn Featured Section for B2B Founders: What to Include
summary: Choose what to feature on your LinkedIn profile, set it up, and give buyers a clearer path to useful resources, credible proof, and a relevant next step.
body_markdown:
The LinkedIn Featured section lets you choose the work a profile visitor sees first. For a B2B founder, a useful starting point is a resource that answers a buying question, evidence that supports your expertise, and a relevant next step. You do not need all three if you only have one strong asset.


Someone who clicks through from your post may understand your opinion but know little about your company. Featured should help that person work out whether your experience applies to their problem.


This guide covers setup, asset selection, example card copy, and a practical way to review what is working.


## What is the LinkedIn Featured section?


Featured is a curated part of a personal LinkedIn profile. It can display posts, articles, external links, and uploaded work samples. Unlike an activity feed, it lets you choose what to keep visible.


There are two important limits. LinkedIn says Featured content is not discoverable through search, and viewers must be signed in to see it. Build this section for people already visiting your profile, rather than treating it as a search-ranking shortcut. See[LinkedIn’s Featured FAQ](https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a552452/featured-section-on-your-profile-faqs) .


For the broader profile, your headline and About section still need to explain who you help. Featured supplies something a visitor can examine.[Rethoric’s guide to working with a LinkedIn profile writer](https://www.rethoric.com/blog-posts/linkedin-profile-writer-for-founders) explains how those pieces fit together.


## How to add the Featured section on LinkedIn


On desktop, follow the path in[LinkedIn’s setup guide](https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a550399/manage-featured-samples-of-your-work-on-your-linkedin-profile) :


1. Open Me, then View Profile.
2. Choose Add profile section, open Recommended, and select Add Featured.
3. Use the Add icon, choose a work-sample type, and follow the prompts.
4. Finish with Save or Done.


In the mobile app, open your profile, tap Add section, then Recommended and Add featured. Choose the sample and save.


To change the order later, open the section’s Edit control and use Reorder. You need at least two items. LinkedIn posts or articles must already be published before you can feature them.


Once the section is live, open every item yourself. Check the destination, access requirements, and mobile presentation before sending people to the profile.


## Choose assets around the visitor’s next question


Start with the person you want to help and the question they are likely to bring. “More leads” is too vague to guide a selection. “A VP of Engineering comparing incident-management tools” gives you something concrete.


Make a short list of existing resources, posts, demos, and approved customer stories. For each, ask: does this help that visitor understand the problem, evaluate our approach, or take a sensible next step?


### A useful resource for someone still evaluating


A checklist, comparison guide, or technical walkthrough can show how you think before a buyer is ready for a call. Choose a resource connected to a decision your company understands.


If you sell incident-management software, a guide to evaluating on-call handoffs is more relevant than a general collection of productivity tips. Include tradeoffs and situations where your approach may not fit. That gives a buyer something to assess.


If you need to build the resource,[Rethoric’s guide to LinkedIn lead magnets](https://www.rethoric.com/blog-posts/linkedin-lead-magnets-b2b-founders) covers choosing a useful format and following up.


### Evidence for someone checking your credibility


Use a customer story, a detailed implementation write-up, or a post that explains a difficult decision. The asset should show what happened and why it matters to the reader.


A recognizable logo without context leaves the buyer guessing. A specific explanation of the initial problem, the work done, and the limits of the outcome is more useful. Obtain permission before using customer names, screenshots, quotes, or results.


If you do not have an approved customer story, show your own work. A product walkthrough using synthetic data is more honest than an anonymous success story assembled from assumptions.[Rethoric’s customer-story guide](https://www.rethoric.com/blog-posts/customer-story-linkedin-post) can help you develop real proof into a post.


### A next step that matches the level of interest


Choose a destination with a clear purpose: watch a workflow, read a service overview, try a product, or book a relevant conversation. A homepage can work if it immediately answers the same question as the card. Otherwise, use a more specific page.


Avoid making every card a request to book a call. A visitor who is still investigating the problem needs a reason to continue, not several versions of the same sales invitation.


## LinkedIn Featured section examples for B2B founders


The examples below are hypothetical. They are not Rethoric client results or claims about conversion performance. Each pairing shows how the same section can serve a different buyer situation.


### Example 1: An early-stage technical founder without customer proof


Imagine a founder building an incident-management tool. The product exists, but there is no approved customer case study yet.


- Resource card: “Before You Replace Your On-Call Workflow.” Description: “A checklist for reviewing escalation ownership, handoff gaps, and migration effort.”
- Demo card: “See an Incident Handoff From Start to Finish.” Description: “A product walkthrough using sample data, including what happens when the first responder is unavailable.”


Start with these two if both are useful. Do not add a weak third item to fill space. The checklist explains the founder’s judgment; the demo lets a buyer inspect the product.


### Example 2: A founder whose buyers need implementation confidence


Suppose the company has an approved customer story about changing an on-call process. Buyers frequently ask how much work a switch will involve.


- Proof card: “How One Engineering Team Changed Its Escalation Process.” Description: “The starting workflow, implementation decisions, and lessons the customer approved for publication.”
- Planning card: “What to Prepare Before an Incident-Management Rollout.” Description: “A practical review of integrations, ownership, and the information your team needs before starting.”


Lead with the story when it addresses the objection buyers keep raising. If you include a metric in the actual asset, explain its measurement period, scope, and relevant limitations. Never turn one customer’s result into a general promise.


### Example 3: A services founder selling a diagnostic engagement


A consultant helping engineering teams improve incident response might lead with a worked example rather than a software demo.


- Worked-example card: “What an On-Call Handoff Review Looks Like.” Description: “An illustrative workflow review showing the questions we ask and how we prioritize changes.”
- Service card: “Incident-Response Review: Scope and Deliverables.” Description: “Who the review is for, what the team needs to provide, and what you receive.”


The service page can offer a conversation after explaining the engagement. If the worked example uses fictional inputs, label them clearly inside the asset as well as on the card.


## Write card copy that helps someone choose


A visitor should be able to tell what they will open without recognizing your company’s internal project names. “Our latest insights” and “Learn more” provide very little information.


Use this simple draft structure:


- Title: the buyer’s task or the concrete thing they will see.
- Description: who it is for, what it covers, and any important condition.
- Destination: the exact resource promised by the title.


For example, replace “Download Our Guide” with “Questions to Ask Before Changing Your On-Call Process.” Replace “See Our Platform” with “Watch How an Incident Gets Escalated.” Use those descriptions only when the linked material actually delivers them.


Keep thumbnail text short enough to read at a glance. Preview the card on a phone and desktop; make sure cropping does not remove the essential words. A simple, legible image is preferable to a miniature slide full of details.


## Order, check, and maintain the section


Put the most useful item first for the audience you are trying to reach now. That may be a resource for an unfamiliar category, an approved customer story for a skeptical buyer, or a demo for someone evaluating a clear use case.


LinkedIn places newly featured material first by default, so check the order after adding an item. There is no reason to let upload order make your editorial decision.


Before calling the section finished, run this short check:


- Relevance: does each item support the audience and problem described in the profile?
- Accuracy: are product details, claims, and service descriptions still current?
- Permissions: are customer materials approved and intended for this audience?
- Access: does each destination work for someone outside your company?
- Clarity: can someone tell what they will get before clicking?


Review the selection when your offer, buyer, or strongest evidence changes. Remove old event registrations and resources you no longer maintain. Keep a small inventory with the asset owner and last review date so the section does not become a forgotten archive.


## Measure useful visits and conversations


For external links to a website you measure, use consistent UTM parameters.[Google’s campaign URL guidance](https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/10917952?hl=en) explains how source, medium, and campaign tags identify referral traffic in Analytics. Add a distinct content value for each Featured link.


An example naming scheme is utm_source=linkedin, utm_medium=organic_social, utm_campaign=founder_profile, and utm_content=featured_demo. Use the scheme your team already follows if it differs.


Review whether those visits reach the intended resource and complete relevant actions, such as viewing a demo or submitting an appropriate inquiry. Also record when someone mentions a Featured asset in a sales conversation.


Treat this as incomplete evidence. Tagged website sessions do not tell you how many people saw a card, and a conversation may involve several touchpoints. Do not label a change in total profile views as proof that one card caused it.


When you revise the section, record what changed and why. If traffic is sparse, buyer feedback may tell you more than a small movement in clicks. Look for a useful pattern before drawing a conclusion.


## Frequently asked questions


### Do I need LinkedIn Premium to use Featured?


The standard work-sample workflow is separate from the subscriber-only “Add content from profile” option. LinkedIn reserves that latter option, which can spotlight details such as Experience or Recommendations, for Premium Business, Sales Navigator, and Recruiter subscribers. Check[LinkedIn’s profile-content guidance](https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a1587673) if that is the option you want.


### How many items should a founder feature?


Start with two or three strong, distinct items if you have them. This is an editorial recommendation, not a LinkedIn limit or a ranking rule. One relevant asset is better than several weak or redundant ones.


### Why can’t someone see my Featured section?


An empty section is hidden. Viewers must also be signed in, and an item’s visibility settings still apply. A connections-only post does not become public simply because you feature it.[LinkedIn’s Featured FAQ](https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a552452/featured-section-on-your-profile-faqs) explains these restrictions.


### Should I feature my most popular post?


Only if it helps the audience you want to reach now. A widely shared personal story may be less useful here than a quieter post that explains a buying decision. Judge the asset by relevance and substance, not its like count.


## Give the right visitor something worth opening


Choose one buyer question, find the strongest honest asset that answers it, and place it where a profile visitor can find it. Add a clear next step when it is useful. You can build from there.
